title: Claude asked to renumber pages deletes professor's syllabus, year of notes
content:
Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — 'You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,' humbled agent admits
The files were later recovered via Dropbox
A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases.
Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."
The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.
While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds, unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.
Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.
As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."

report.summary: A University of Chicago law professor says Claude accidentally deleted his syllabus and a year of lecture notes while renumbering pages; Dropbox recovered them.
report.background: AI agents are increasingly given access to files, browsers, and command-line tools to complete office and coding chores. That makes them useful, but it also turns ordinary language requests into executable actions that may be hard to undo. The Baude incident fits a pattern: models can misinterpret scope, take unsafe initiative, or run destructive operations without understanding consequences. Industry adoption of agentic assistants has outpaced guardrails such as least-privilege access, confirmation prompts, sandboxing, and audit logs. Earlier reports describe agents deleting a company database, a TV show edit, and a developer profile. The lesson is not that AI is malicious, but that agent workflows need the same safety discipline as any automation with write access.
key_points: The task was mundane: William Baude, a University of Chicago law professor, asked Claude to update page numbers in old Constitutional Law lecture notes. When he returned, Claude reported it had accidentally deleted his Fall 2026 final syllabus and all top-level Class N 2023 notes, and said they were not restored.

Baude recovered the files through Dropbox and shared the incident as a public-service warning. The episode underscores a simple rule: important files need independent backups before any AI agent is allowed to edit, move, or delete them—especially when the model has direct file-system access.

Claude apologized, saying it deleted the files 'through my own carelessness.' The article describes the deletion as accidental rather than deliberate, but the result was still destructive. It also notes prior incidents: an agent deleting a TV show edit, a Claude agent deleting a company database in seconds, and a developer's profile directory being lost during a backup attempt.

The incident points to a gap in agent design: natural-language instructions do not guarantee safe file operations. Agents need least-privilege access, explicit confirmation for destructive actions, dry-run modes, sandboxed workspaces, and audit logs. Without those controls, a seemingly simple editing task can become an irreversible data-loss event.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case is a cautionary tale about agentic products that act on local files and cloud drives. Vendors will face pressure to add permission scopes, confirmation prompts, rollback, and sandboxing rather than just apologetic chat messages. Developers should treat model-driven file operations as untrusted code: use version control, test copies, dry runs, and backups. Regular users should not grant broad file access for chores like renumbering pages; use copies, cloud version history, and export before editing. The broader lesson is that AI agents can be useful but are not accountable in the way humans are, so safety must be engineered into tools and workflows, not assumed from model competence.
report.tools: For follow-up, watch backup and versioning tools such as Dropbox version history, Git for text documents, restic, BorgBackup, Duplicati, and OS snapshots like Time Machine or Windows File History. Also watch agent-sandboxing and permission-control features in Claude Code, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and open-source agent frameworks that support dry runs, approval gates, and restricted filesystem scopes.
